title: Book: Common Stocks and Uncommon Profits — Philip Fisher (1958)
publisher: Artha Kavach original summary of a book's ideas (paraphrase, not a quotation; the author's opinion, not settled fact) — pending manual verification
text: Philip Fisher argued for buying outstanding growth companies and holding them for a long time. His distinctive method is 'scuttlebutt': gather information by talking to customers, suppliers, competitors and former employees, not just reading financial statements. He listed fifteen points to judge a company, including management quality, research and development, sales strength and profit margins, and he preferred to hold a small number of stocks he knew well. Buffett has credited him as an influence. Cautions: it takes extensive research, concentrated portfolios are risky, and it is a mid-twentieth-century US book; for beginners it is a way to understand how quality is judged, not a how-to.
